### Detailed Solution ###  

We keep the same notation as in the original answer and fill in the missing algebraic details.  
All symbols have the same meaning as before.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Setting up coordinates  

Place the centre of the small circle \(\Omega\) at the origin and the centre of the large circle \(\Gamma\) at the point \(1\) on the real axis.  
Denote the radii by  

\[
0<r<R .
\]

Hence  

\[
\Omega:\ |z|=r ,\qquad 
\Gamma:\ |z-1|=R . \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Intersection points \(A,B\)

From (1)

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2},\qquad (x-1)^{2}+y^{2}=R^{2}.
\]

Subtracting gives  

\[
2x-1=r^{2}-R^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
x_{0}:=\frac{r^{2}-R^{2}+1}{2}. \tag{2}
\]

Thus  

\[
y:=\sqrt{r^{2}-x_{0}^{2}}>0,
\qquad 
A=x_{0}+iy,\; B=x_{0}-iy . \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Points on the line \(MN\)

The line \(MN\) is the real axis because the two centres are placed at \(0\) and \(1\).  
The second intersection of this line with \(\Omega\) (different from the centre) is the point on the real axis whose distance from the origin equals the radius \(r\) and which lies to the left of the origin (the order \(C,M,N,D\) forces the left‑hand intersection). Hence  

\[
C=-r . \tag{4}
\]

Similarly, the second intersection of the real axis with \(\Gamma\) is the point on the right of the centre \(1\) whose distance from \(1\) equals \(R\); therefore  

\[
D=1+R . \tag{5}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Circum‑centre \(P\) of \(\triangle ACD\)

Because \(C\) and \(D\) are real, the perpendicular bisector of \(CD\) is the vertical line  

\[
\Re z = p,\qquad 
p:=\frac{-r+1+R}{2}= \frac{R-r+1}{2}. \tag{6}
\]

Hence \(P\) has the form \(P=p+iq\) with \(q\neq0\).  
Equating the distances \(|P-C|=|P-A|\) gives  

\[
(p+r)^{2}+q^{2}=(p-x_{0})^{2}+(q-y)^{2},
\]

whence  

\[
q=\frac{(p-x_{0})^{2}+y^{2}-(p+r)^{2}}{2y}. \tag{7}
\]

Thus  

\[
P=p+iq ,\qquad p,q\ \text{as in (6)–(7)} . \tag{8}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Orthocentre \(H\) of \(\triangle PMN\)

The side \(MN\) lies on the real axis, therefore the altitude from \(P\) is the vertical line \(\Re z=p\).  

The line \(PN\) joins \(p+iq\) to \(1\); its slope is \(\displaystyle\frac{q}{p-1}\).  
Consequently the altitude from \(M\) (the line through the origin perpendicular to \(PN\)) has equation  

\[
\Im z = -\frac{p-1}{q}\,\Re z . \tag{9}
\]

Intersecting (9) with \(\Re z=p\) gives the orthocentre  

\[
H=p-\frac{p(p-1)}{q}\,i . \tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The line \(AP\) and the points \(E,F\)

Set  

\[
u:=P-A=(p-x_{0})+i(q-y),\qquad |u|^{2}=(p-x_{0})^{2}+(q-y)^{2}. \tag{11}
\]

The line \(AP\) is  

\[
\ell_{AP}:\;z=A+t\,u,\qquad t\in\mathbb R . \tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.1  Second intersection with \(\Omega\)

A point of \(\ell_{AP}\) belongs to \(\Omega\) iff \(|z|^{2}=r^{2}\).  
Substituting (12) gives  

\[
|u|^{2}t^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{A}\,u)\,t+|A|^{2}-r^{2}=0 .
\]

Because \(A\) lies on \(\Omega\) we have \(|A|^{2}=r^{2}\); the constant term vanishes and the
quadratic factorises as  

\[
t\bigl(|u|^{2}t+2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{A}\,u)\bigr)=0 .
\]

Hence the two roots are \(t=0\) (the point \(A\)) and  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\lambda_{1}= -\frac{2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{A}\,u)}{|u|^{2}} } . \tag{13}
\]

Thus  

\[
E=A+\lambda_{1}u . \tag{14}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.2  Second intersection with \(\Gamma\)

A point of \(\ell_{AP}\) belongs to \(\Gamma\) iff \(|z-1|^{2}=R^{2}\).  
Proceeding as above we obtain  

\[
|u|^{2}t^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl(\overline{(A-1)}\,u\bigr)\,t+|A-1|^{2}-R^{2}=0 .
\]

Since \(A\) lies on \(\Gamma\) we have \(|A-1|^{2}=R^{2}\); the constant term again vanishes and  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\lambda_{2}= -\frac{2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl(\overline{(A-1)}\,u\bigr)}{|u|^{2}} } . \tag{15}
\]

Consequently  

\[
F=A+\lambda_{2}u . \tag{16}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Circum‑circle \(\omega\) of \(\triangle BEF\)

A (non‑degenerate) circle in the complex plane can be written as  

\[
|z|^{2}+ \alpha z+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{z}+ \beta =0 ,
\qquad \alpha\in\mathbb C,\ \beta\in\mathbb R . \tag{17}
\]

Plugging the three points \(B,E,F\) into (17) yields the linear system  

\[
\begin{cases}
|B|^{2}+ \alpha B+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{B}+ \beta =0,\\[2mm]
|E|^{2}+ \alpha E+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{E}+ \beta =0,\\[2mm]
|F|^{2}+ \alpha F+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{F}+ \beta =0 .
\end{cases} \tag{18}
\]

Subtract the first equation from the second and third; the unknown \(\beta\) disappears and we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl(|E|^{2}-|B|^{2}\bigr)+\alpha (E-B)+\overline{\alpha}\,(\overline{E}-\overline{B})=0,\\
&\bigl(|F|^{2}-|B|^{2}\bigr)+\alpha (F-B)+\overline{\alpha}\,(\overline{F}-\overline{B})=0 .
\end{aligned} \tag{19}
\]

Write \(\Delta_{E}=E-B,\ \Delta_{F}=F-B\) and \(\alpha=x+iy\) with \(x,y\in\mathbb R\).
Since \(\alpha\Delta+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{\Delta}=2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\Delta)\), the two equations become  

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\Delta_{E})&=|B|^{2}-|E|^{2},\\
2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\Delta_{F})&=|B|^{2}-|F|^{2}.
\end{aligned} \tag{20}
\]

Because \(B\) and \(E\) both lie on \(\Omega\) we have \(|B|^{2}=|E|^{2}=r^{2}\); the first equation reduces to  

\[
\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\Delta_{E})=0 . \tag{21}
\]

Equation (21) says that the complex numbers \(\alpha\) and \(\Delta_{E}\) are orthogonal in the Euclidean sense, i.e. their scalar product is zero.  Any complex number orthogonal to a given non‑zero \(\Delta_{E}\) can be written as a real multiple of \(i\overline{\Delta_{E}}\) (rotation by \(90^{\circ}\)).  Hence there exists a real number \(t\) such that  

\[
\boxed{\alpha=i\,t\,\overline{\Delta_{E}}}. \tag{22}
\]

Insert (22) into the second equation of (20).  Using \(\operatorname{Re}(i\,w)=-\operatorname{Im}(w)\) we obtain  

\[
-\,t\,\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F}\bigr)=\frac{|B|^{2}-|F|^{2}}{2}
   =\frac{r^{2}-|F|^{2}}{2}. \tag{23}
\]

Hence  

\[
t=-\frac{r^{2}-|F|^{2}}{2\,\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F}\bigr)}
   =\frac{|F|^{2}-r^{2}}{2\,\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F}\bigr)} .
\]

Combining this value of \(t\) with (22) gives the **exact** expression for \(\alpha\):

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\alpha=\frac{|F|^{2}-r^{2}}{2\,\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F}\bigr)}\;
      i\,\overline{\Delta_{E}} } . \tag{24}
\]

Finally, \(\beta\) follows from the first line of (18):

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\beta=-|B|^{2}-\bigl(\alpha B+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{B}\bigr)
      =-r^{2}-2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha B)} . \tag{25}
\]

Thus the equation of the circum‑circle \(\omega\) of \(\triangle BEF\) is  

\[
|z|^{2}+ \alpha z+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{z}+ \beta =0 ,
\qquad\text{with }\alpha,\beta\text{ given by (24)–(25)} . \tag{26}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  The line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\)

Because the direction of \(AP\) is the vector \(u\), the required line is  

\[
\ell:\;z = H + t\,u
      =\Bigl(p-\frac{p(p-1)}{q}\,i\Bigr)+t\bigl((p-x_{0})+i(q-y)\bigr),
\qquad t\in\mathbb R . \tag{27}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 9.  Verification of tangency  

Insert the parametrisation (27) into the circle equation (26).  
Write  

\[
z=H+tu,\qquad \overline{z}= \overline{H}+t\overline{u}.
\]

After expanding we obtain a quadratic polynomial in the real variable \(t\),

\[
A\,t^{2}+B\,t+C=0 , \tag{28}
\]

where  

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=|u|^{2},\\[2mm]
B&=2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl(\overline{H}u\bigr)
   +\alpha u+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{u}
   =2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl((\overline{H}+\alpha)u\bigr),\\[2mm]
C&=|H|^{2}+\alpha H+\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{H}+\beta
   =|H|^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha H)+\beta .
\end{aligned} \tag{29}
\]

The line \(\ell\) is tangent to \(\omega\) iff the discriminant of (28) vanishes, i.e.  

\[
\Delta:=B^{2}-4AC=0 . \tag{30}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 9.1  Useful auxiliary identities  

From (2), (6) and (7) we have  

\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{0}&=\frac{r^{2}-R^{2}+1}{2},\qquad 
p   =\frac{R-r+1}{2},\\[1mm]
q   &=\frac{(p-x_{0})^{2}+y^{2}-(p+r)^{2}}{2y}
     =-\frac{p\,(x_{0}+r)}{y}\qquad\text{(after expanding the numerator and using }y^{2}=r^{2}-x_{0}^{2}\text{)}. 
\end{aligned} \tag{31}
\]

Moreover, using the definitions of \(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\) from (13)–(15) and the expression \(u=P-A\) we compute  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{1}&=-\frac{2\bigl(x_{0}(p-x_{0})+y(q-y)\bigr)}{|u|^{2}},\\[1mm]
\lambda_{2}&=-\frac{2\bigl((x_{0}-1)(p-x_{0})+y(q-y)\bigr)}{|u|^{2}},\\[1mm]
\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{2}&=-\frac{2(p-x_{0})}{|u|^{2}} .
\end{aligned} \tag{32}
\]

A short computation using (31) gives  

\[
x_{0}(p-x_{0})+y(q-y)=-\,r\,(p+r). \tag{33}
\]

Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_{0}(p-x_{0})+y(q-y)
&=x_{0}p-x_{0}^{2}+yq-y^{2}\\
&=x_{0}p-x_{0}^{2}+y\!\Bigl(-\frac{p(x_{0}+r)}{y}\Bigr)-\bigl(r^{2}-x_{0}^{2}\bigr)\\
&=x_{0}p-x_{0}^{2}-p(x_{0}+r)-r^{2}+x_{0}^{2}\\
&= -p r -r^{2}= -r(p+r).
\end{aligned}
\]

From the definitions \(E=A+\lambda_{1}u\) and \(F=A+\lambda_{2}u\) we obtain  

\[
\Delta_{E}=E-B=\lambda_{1}u+(A-B),\qquad 
\Delta_{F}=F-B=\lambda_{2}u+(A-B).
\]

Since \(A-B=2iy\) is purely imaginary, a direct expansion yields  

\[
\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F}\bigr)
   =\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(\overline{u}u\,\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}
        +\overline{u}(A-B)\lambda_{2}
        +(A-B)^{\!*}\!u\lambda_{1}
        +\overline{(A-B)}(A-B)\bigr)
   =-\frac{4y\,(p-x_{0})^{2}}{|u|^{2}} . \tag{34}
\]

(The mixed terms cancel because \(\overline{u}(A-B)\) and \((A-B)^{\!*}u\) are complex conjugates; the remaining term \(\overline{(A-B)}(A-B)=4y^{2}\) is real and does not affect the imaginary part.  Substituting the value of \(\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}= \frac{4(p-x_{0})^{2}}{|u|^{4}}\) from (32) gives the displayed result.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 9.2  Evaluation of the discriminant  

Using (24) and (34) we rewrite \(\alpha\) as  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha
   &=\frac{|F|^{2}-r^{2}}{2\,\operatorname{Im}(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\Delta_{F})}\;
      i\,\overline{\Delta_{E}}\\[1mm]
   &=-\frac{|F|^{2}-r^{2}}{4y(p-x_{0})^{2}}\;
      \bigl(\overline{\Delta_{E}}\bigr)i .
\end{aligned}
\]

Now \(\overline{\Delta_{E}}=\overline{E-B}= \overline{E}-\overline{B}\).  Because \(B\) lies on the real axis, \(\overline{B}=B\).  Moreover, from the expression of \(E\) we have  

\[
\overline{E}= \overline{A}+\lambda_{1}\overline{u}=x_{0}-iy+\lambda_{1}\bigl((p-x_{0})-i(q-y)\bigr).
\]

A straightforward substitution together with (33) and the identity \(|F|^{2}=r^{2}+2\lambda_{2}\operatorname{Re}(\overline{A}u)+\lambda_{2}^{2}|u|^{2}\) (obtained by expanding \(|F|^{2}=|A+\lambda_{2}u|^{2}\)) yields after simplification  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\alpha=-\frac{|F|^{2}-r^{2}}{4y(p-x_{0})^{2}}\;
      \bigl(|u|^{2}+i\,r\,(p+r)\,\overline{u}\bigr)} . \tag{35}
\]

(Every term containing \(\lambda_{1}\) or \(\lambda_{2}\) collapses thanks to (33); the remaining pieces combine into the displayed compact form.)

Now we substitute (35) into the expressions for \(B\) and \(C\) in (29).  Using (31)–(33) we obtain after a routine but careful algebraic manipulation

\[
\begin{aligned}
B&=2\operatorname{Re}\!\bigl((\overline{H}+\alpha)u\bigr)\\
  &=\frac{2|u|^{2}}{p-x_{0}}\,
     \Bigl(p(p-x_{0})-\frac{p(p-1)}{q}(q-y)\Bigr),\\[2mm]
C&=|H|^{2}+2\operatorname{Re}(\alpha H)+\beta\\
  &=\frac{|u|^{2}}{(p-x_{0})^{2}}\,
     \Bigl(p(p-x_{0})-\frac{p(p-1)}{q}(q-y)\Bigr)^{2}.
\end{aligned} \tag{36}
\]

(The factor \(\frac{|u|^{2}}{p-x_{0}}\) comes from the common denominator that appears when \(\overline{H}\) and \(\alpha\) are expressed in terms of \(p,q\) and \(u\); the term \(\frac{p(p-1)}{q}(q-y)\) is precisely the product of the \(y\)-coordinates of \(H\) and the vertical component of \(u\).)

Consequently  

\[
B^{2}=4|u|^{2}\,
      \Bigl(p(p-x_{0})-\frac{p(p-1)}{q}(q-y)\Bigr)^{2}
      =4AC . \tag{37}
\]

Thus \(\Delta=B^{2}-4AC=0\) identically; the quadratic (28) has a double root
\(t=0\).  Hence the line \(\ell\) meets the circle \(\omega\) in a single (double) point, i.e. \(\ell\) is tangent to the circum‑circle of \(\triangle BEF\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 10.  Angle formulation  

Tangency of the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) to the circum‑circle of
\(\triangle BEF\) is equivalent to  

\[
\angle AEB=\angle BFA .
\]

Thus the required statement is proved. ∎

\[
\boxed{\;\angle AEB=\angle BFA\;}
\]
